Load required packages:
```{r, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(misty)
library(ggplot2)
library(jtools)
library(rstatix)
library(knitr)
library(Rmisc)
```
Import processed data:
```{r}
dat <- read.csv2('Data/Study2_data_processed.csv')
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Turn the id and group variables into factors and add labels to the groups.
dat <-
  dat %>% 
  mutate(id = factor(id),
         condition = factor(condition, 
                            levels = c('3', '1', '2'), 
                            labels = c('Control', 'Harmonious', 'Conflicting'))
         )
```

# On-line health and taste ratings

First, we tested whether participants paid attention to the high and low taste and health ratings of individual meals in the different contexts and base rate manipulations. We conducted a mixed ANOVA with the recalled mean rating as outcome, context (first vs. second), rating type (taste vs. health) as within-subject factors, and base rate manipulation (harmonious vs. conflicting vs. control) as between-subjects factor. Of special interest was the 3-way interaction between base rate manipulation, context and rating type.

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=TRUE}
# Restructure mean on-line ratings from wide into long format for repeated measures ANOVA, convert the context and rating type variables into factors. 
dat_onl <- 
  dat %>% 
  select(id, condition, starts_with('mean_onl')) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(id, condition),
               names_to = 'trial',
               values_to = 'rating') %>%
  mutate(context = case_when(grepl('c1', trial) ~ 1,
                             grepl('c2', trial) ~ 2) ,
         rating_type = case_when(grepl('taste', trial) ~ 1,
                                 grepl('health', trial) ~ 2)
  ) %>% 
  mutate(context = factor(context,
                          levels = c('1', '2'),
                          labels= c('1st Context', '2nd Context')),
         rating_type = factor(rating_type,
                              levels = c('1', '2'),
                              labels= c('Taste Rating', 'Health Rating'))
  )
  
```

## Descriptive statistics

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Check the mean, standard deviation, standard error and 95% confidence interval of the on-line health and taste ratings in each base rate manipulation and context.
onl_sum <- summarySE(dat_onl, measurevar="rating", groupvars=c('condition', 'context', 'rating_type'))
onl_sum %>% 
  kable(format = 'markdown', digits = 2,
        col.names = c('Base rate manipulation', 'Context', 'Rating type', 'N', 'Mean rating', 'Std. Dev.', 'Std. Error', '95% CI'), 
        caption = 'Mean health and taste ratings by base rate manipulation and context')

```

## ANOVA

```{r}
aov_onl <-
  anova_test(
    data = dat_onl, 
    dv = rating,
    wid = id,
    within = c(context, rating_type),
    between = condition, type = 3, effect.size = 'pes')

```
``` {r, include=FALSE}
colnames(aov_onl) <- c('Effect','df/nominator', 'df/denominator', '$F$', '$p$', 'Sig.', 'partial $\\eta^2$')
rownames(aov_onl) <- c('Base rate manipulation', 'Context', 'Rating type', 'Base rate manipulation*Context', 'Base rate manipulation*Rating type', 'Context*Rating type', 'Base rate manipulation\\*Context\\*Rating type')

```
``` {r, echo=FALSE}
kable(aov_onl[, -1], format = 'markdown', digits = 2)
```

## Follow-up: 3-way interaction

There was large effect of the 3-way interaction, indicating that the ratings differed depending on the rating type (health vs. taste), the context (1st vs. 2nd) and the base rate manipulation (harmonious vs. conflicting vs. control).
To follow up, we calculated pairwise comparisons, using Bonferroni corrections, of the ratings between the two contexts at all combinations of base rate manipulation and rating type.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
onl_pw <- 
  dat_onl %>%
  group_by(condition, rating_type) %>%
  pairwise_t_test(rating ~ context, p.adjust.method = "bonferroni")

kable(onl_pw[,-c(3:7)], format = 'markdown', digits = 2,
      caption = 'Pairwise comparisons of taste and health on-line ratings between contexts within each base rate manipulation',
      col.names = c('Base rate manipulation', 'Rating', '$p$', 'Sign', '$p.adj$', 'Sign. adj.'))
```

## Plot the results

```{r, echo=FALSE}
onl_sum %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = context, y = rating, group = rating_type)) + 
  geom_line(stat="identity",
            aes(color = rating_type, 
                linetype = rating_type),
            size = 1) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=rating-ci, ymax=rating+ci),
                width=.2) +
  geom_point(aes(color = rating_type, 
                 shape = rating_type),
             size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(facets = 'condition') +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1, 5))+
  theme_apa() +
  labs(x = 'Context', y = 'Mean Rating',
       title ='On-line Health and Taste Ratings')+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.position = 'top',
        axis.title.y = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 16),
        axis.title.x = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 16),
        text = element_text(size = 16))

```

# Base rate estimates

Finally, we tested whether participants correctly recognized the high and low base rates of healthy and tasty food in the different contexts and base rate manipulations. We conducted a mixed ANOVA with the estimated number of foods as outcome, context (first vs. second), estimate type (tasty vs. healthy foods) as within-subject factors, and base rate manipulation (harmonious vs. conflicting vs. control) as between-subjects factor. Again, we were mainly interested in the 3-way interaction between base rate manipulation, context and estimate type.

Participants estimated the numbers of healthy and tasty as well as unhealthy and not tasty food. But as the estimates for healthy + unhealthy and tasty + not tasty food had to amount to the overall number of presented foods per context, we only analysed the estimates of tasty and healthy, but not not tasty and unhealthy foods, as this would have been redundant.

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Restructure health and taste base rate estimates from wide into long format for repeated measures ANOVA, convert the context and rating type variables into factors. 
dat_base <-
  dat %>% 
  select(id, condition, starts_with(c('base_tasty','base_healthy'))) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(id, condition),
               names_to = 'trial',
               values_to = 'estimate') %>% 
  mutate(context = case_when(grepl('c1', trial) ~ 1,
                             grepl('c2', trial) ~ 2),
         estimate_type = case_when(grepl('base_tasty', trial) ~ 1,
                                  grepl('base_healthy', trial) ~ 2)
         ) %>%
  mutate(context = factor(context,
                          levels = c('1', '2'),
                          labels= c('1st Context', '2nd Context')),
         estimate_type = factor(estimate_type,
                               levels = c('1', '2'),
                               labels= c('Tasty Food', 'Healthy Food'))
        )
         

```

## Descriptive statistics

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Check the mean, standard deviation, standard error and 95% confidence interval of the base rate estimates for each base rate manipulation, context and rating type
base_sum <- summarySE(dat_base, measurevar='estimate', groupvars=c('condition', 'context', 'estimate_type'))
base_sum %>% 
  kable(format = 'markdown', digits = 2,
        col.names = c('Base rate manipulation', 'Context', 'Estimate type','N', 'Mean estimate', 'Std. Dev.', 'Std. Error', '95% CI'), 
        caption = 'Mean base rate estimates by base rate manipulation, context and estimate type')

```

## ANOVA

``` {r}
aov_base <-
  anova_test(
    data = dat_base, 
    dv = estimate,
    wid = id,
    within = c(context, estimate_type),
    between = condition, type = 3, effect.size = 'pes')
```

``` {r, include=FALSE}
colnames(aov_base) <- c('Effect','df/nominator', 'df/denominator', '$F$', '$p$', 'Sig.', 'partial $\\eta^2$')
rownames(aov_base) <- c('Base rate manipulation', 'Context', 'Estimate type', 'Base rate manipulation*Context', 'Base rate manipulation*Estimate type', 'Context*Estimate type', 'Base rate manipulation\\*Context\\*Estimate type')

```
``` {r, echo=FALSE}
kable(aov_base[, -1], format = 'markdown', digits = 2)
```


## Follow-up: 3-way interaction

There was large effect of the 3-way interaction, indicating that the base rate estimates depended on the base rate manipulation, the context, as well as whether participants estimated the base rates of tasty or healthy food. 
To follow up, we calculated pairwise comparisons, using Bonferroni corrections, of the base rate estimates between the two contexts at all combinations of base rate manipulation and estimate type.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
base_pw <- 
  dat_base %>%
  group_by(condition, estimate_type) %>%
  pairwise_t_test(estimate ~ context, p.adjust.method = "bonferroni")

kable(base_pw[,-c(3:7)], format = 'markdown', digits = 2,
        caption = 'Pairwise comparisons of estimates of tasty and healthy foods between contexts within each base rate manipulation and estimate type',
        col.names = c('Base rate manipulation', 'Estimate', '$p$', 'Sign', '$p.adj$', 'Sign. adj.'))
```

## Plot the results

``` {r, echo=FALSE}
base_sum %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = context, y = estimate, group = estimate_type)) +
  stat_summary(geom = 'line', 
               aes(color = estimate_type, 
                   linetype = estimate_type), 
               fun = identity,
               size = 1) +
  stat_summary(geom = 'point',
               aes(color = estimate_type, 
                   shape = estimate_type),
               size = 3,
               fun = identity) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=estimate-ci, ymax=estimate+ci),
                width=.2)+
  facet_wrap(facets = 'condition')+
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 10)) +
  theme_apa() +
  labs(x = 'Context', 
       y = 'Mean Estimate',
       title = 'Base Rate Estimates') +
  theme(legend.position = 'top', plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        axis.title.y = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 18),
        axis.title.x = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 18),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 18),
        text = element_text(size = 16)) +
  scale_color_discrete(name = 'Estimate Type', labels = c('Tasty Food', 'Healthy Food')) +
  scale_shape_discrete(name = 'Estimate Type', labels = c('Tasty Food', 'Healthy Food')) +
  scale_linetype_discrete(name = 'Estimate Type', labels = c('Tasty Food', 'Healthy Food'))

```

# Summary of results

The analyses of the on-line ratings show that participants viewing harmonious base rates correctly rated the food as both healthier and tastier in the first than second context. Participants viewing conflicting base rates correctly rated the food as tastier, but less healthy in the first than second context. Participants in the control group incorrectly rated the food as healthier and tastier in the second than first context, but the difference was very small.

The analyses of the base rate estimates show that participants viewing harmonious base rates estimated more tasty and healthy foods in the first compared with the second context. Conversely, participants viewing conflicting base rates estimated more tasty and less healthy foods in the first compared with the second context. In the control group, base rate estimates of healthy and tasty foods did not differ between contexts. 

That means participants paid attention to the individual high and low health and taste ratings in the different contexts and base rate manipulations. They also correctly identified the skewed health and taste base rates in the respective contexts and base rate manipulations.
